sec.title: Background
sec.p: Plague and tularemia are endemic rodent-borne zoonoses in Iran. This study investigated their presence of these diseases in wildlife populations in southern Iran. Sheepdogs were also surveyed as sentinel animals to provide early warning of potential outbreaks.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: In August 2018, sampling involved the capturing rodents and collecting blood from wild carnivores and sheepdogs. Rodent spleen tissues and ectoparasites were analyzed using real-time PCR to detect Yersinia pestis (targeting the yihN, pla, and caf1 genes) and Francisella tularensis (targeting the ISFtu2 and fopA genes). All tissue samples underwent bacterial isolation. Additionally, rodents, wild carnivores, and sheepdogs were screened for specific antibodies to assess pathogen exposure.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 65 rodents were captured, primarily Rattus rattus (35.38%), Tatera indica (29.23%), and Acomys dimidiatus (20%). Serological surveys included 35 domestic sheepdogs (Canis lupus familiaris), 4 jackals (Canis aureus), and 3 Indian grey mongooses (Urva edwardsi). Thirty fleas, all of the genus Xenopsylla, were collected as ectoparasites. All samples tested negative for tularemia via agglutination assay. No wild mammals showed seropositivity, but plague-specific antibodies were detected in 4 sheepdogs (11.42%). Molecular tests and bacterial cultures for both plague and tularemia were negative.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The presence of plague-specific antibodies in sheepdogs suggest possible plague circulation in southern Iran, indicating a potential risk of human exposure.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Yersinia pestis, the causative agent of plague, is a gram-negative, non-motile, and non-spore-forming coccobacillus from the Enterobacteriaceae family, primarily residing in rodent reservoirs and transmitted mainly by fleas. Despite a decline in plague incidence in recent decades, Y. pestis persists in wildlife across North and South America, Asia, and Africa. Its prolonged presence in animal reservoirs, coupled with emerging antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and multidrug resistance (MDR), underscores the need for ongoing surveillance due to the risk of sudden outbreaks [1]. Molecular diagnosis of Y. pestis faces challenges due to the limited specificity of common genetic markers. Plasmid-encoded genes like pla (pPCP1) and caf1 (pMT1) are highly sensitive due to their high copy number but have been detected in other Enterobacteriaceae, risking false positives [2]. A multi-target approach, incorporating the chromosomal yihN gene, which is unique to Y. pestis, enhances diagnostic specificity. The plague reached southern Iran via ports and cargo ships in the late 18th and early 19th centuries CE [3]. Current data on historical plague foci in southern Iran are limited.

Tularemia, caused by the highly infectious intracellular bacterium Francisella tularensis, is a zoonotic disease transmitted through direct contact with infected animals, ingestion of contaminated water, or arthropod vectors. This facultative intracellular pathogen resides in small mammal like rabbits, squirrels, and voles, which serve as natural reservoirs. Several tick species, including Dermacentor marginatus [4], Ixodes Ricinus [5], Haemaphysalis inermis [5], Rhipicephalus turanicus [5], Rhipicephalus bursa [5], Rhipicephalus sanguineus sensu lato [5], Rhipicephalus anulatus [5], Haemaphysalis concinna [4], Hyalomma marginatum [5], Hyalomma analiticum [5], and Hyalomma aegyptium [6], have been reported as carriers in Iran. Human tularemia cases in Iran have historically been underreported, but recent clinically confirmed cases over the past five years highlight underdiagnosis [7]. A 2023 systematic review in Iran analyzed 1,242 human, 1,565 animal, and 355 surface water samples collected from 2010 to 2020 across 18 provinces, detecting the pathogen in 94 human, 26 animal, and 69 water samples, underscoring its widespread distribution [8]. Molecular diagnosis of F. tularensis is complicated by low bacterial loads, requiring highly specific markers. The multi-copy insertion sequence ISFtu2 enhances sensitivity, while the chromosomal gene fopA ensures species specificity [9]. Wildlife surveillance is critical for identifying endemic and emerging tularemia hotspots in southern Iran.

This study primarily investigated the historical sylvatic plague epicenter in Hormozgan Province, southern Iran, while also assessing tularemia presence through surveys of rodents, wild carnivores, sheepdogs, and arthropod vectors.

sec.title: Study area
sec.p: Hormozgan Province, located in southern Iran along the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, spans 70,697 km² and has a population of approximately 2.5 million. The province features diverse landscapes, including coastal regions, mountain ranges, and arid deserts, with a hot and humid climate. Bandar Abbas, the provincial capital, is a key hub for maritime activities and industries. The study area is depicted in Fig. 1.

sec.title: Ethics statement
sec.p: This study received ethical approval from Ethics Committee of the Pasteur Institute of Iran (IR.PII.REC.1395.9). Measures were implemented to minimize animal suffering and discomfort during all procedures. Rodents were euthanized following AVMA guidelines [10]. All dog owners were briefed on the study’s objectives and sampling procedures. Written informed consent was obtained from each owner prior to the inclusion of their animals in the study.

sec.title: Sampling
sec.p: From August 9 to August 18, 2018, 18 regions in Hormozgan Province were surveyed using live mousetraps baited with nuts, with an average of 153 traps deployed daily. Captured rodents were examined for ectoparasites, which were collected and stored at 4–8 °C for laboratory transport. Cardiac puncture was performed to collect blood, and autopsies were conducted under Biosafety Level 3 (BSL-3) protocols. Spleen tissues, critical for macrophage accumulation and intracellular bacterial replication, were aseptically collected and transported in Cary Blair medium at 4 °C. Blood samples from privately owned sheepdogs, and wild carnivores were collected via the cephalic vein. Blood samples were centrifuged at 2000 × g for 10 min, and sera were stored at -20 °C for analysis.

sec.title: Species identification
sec.p: Rodents were identified through detailed morphological examination following established protocols [11, 12]. Ectoparasites were identified using taxonomic keys under a stereomicroscope (Olympus SZ61, Olympus Corporation, Japan) [13, 14].

sec.title: Microscopic analysis
sec.p: Spleen tissues were screened for Y. pestis using the Wayson staining method to detect bacilli with characteristic bipolar (safety-pin) morphology, though not exclusively specific to Y. pestis. A portion of spleen tissue was homogenized in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, pH 7.4; Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) to create a uniform suspension. A thin smear was prepared on a glass slide (Menzel-Gläser, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Germany), air-dried, and heat-fixed by passing through a Bunsen burner flame three times. The slide was then flooded with Wayson stain solution (BioGnost, Croatia) and incubated at room temperature for 5 min. The smears were gently rinsed with PBS to remove excess stains and subsequently air-dried thoroughly. The stained smear was analyzed under oil immersion at 1000× magnification using a compound light microscope (Olympus BX43, Olympus Corporation, Japan). Bacilli exhibiting the characteristic bipolar (safety-pin) staining pattern were documented as presumptive Y. pestis [15].

sec.title: Bacterial culture
sec.p: Spleen and flea samples were processed for bacterial isolation. Spleen samples were homogenized in 5 mL of normal saline, and 50 µL of the homogenate was immediately inoculated onto three culture media: Yersinia Selective Agar [15] supplemented with cefsulodin, irgasan, and novobiocin (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany); Sheep Blood Agar [15] (Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany); Cystine Heart Agar, supplemented with chocolatized red blood cells, polymyxin B, amphotericin B, and vancomycin [16] (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., Waltham, MA, USA), optimized for Y. pestis and F. tularensis isolation. Ectoparasite were surface-sterilized by immersion in 1 mL of 70% ethanol for 3 min, followed by three sequential washes with 1 mL of sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) for 3 min each. Subsequently, each ectoparasite were individually macerated using sterile pestles to yield a homogeneous suspension, and 500 µL of homogenate was inoculated onto the aforementioned culture media under sterile conditions.

Cultures were incubated under controlled conditions: 37 °C in a 5% CO₂ humidified atmosphere for F. tularensis [16] and 30 °C for Y. pestis [15]. Plates were inspected daily for 10 day. Colonies exhibiting morphological characteristics indicative of the target pathogens were subjected to initial biochemical characterization, including catalase, oxidase, motility, urease, and indole tests. Isolates were then screened using molecular techniques.

sec.title: Serological assays
sec.p: Serological analysis was performed on rodents, sheepdogs, and wild carnivores to evaluate prior exposure to Y. pestis and F. tularensis. A qualitative in-house enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) was utilized to detect IgG antibodies specific to the F1 capsular antigen of Y. pestis [17]. All reagents, including control sera, antigens, and conjugated antibodies, were procured from the Pasteur Institute of Madagascar (WHO Collaborating Centre for Plague) and processed according to their validated protocols. For anti-F1 IgG detection, 96-well ELISA plates (PolySorp, Nunc, Germany) were coated with F1 antigen (3.8 µg/mL, 70 µL/well) in carbonate buffer (pH 9.6) and incubated overnight at 4 °C. Plates were washed with PBS/0.1% Tween 20, blocked with PBS/0.1% Tween 20/5% skim milk at 37 °C for 2 h, and washed again. Serum samples, diluted 1:100 in PBS/0.1% Tween 20/5% skim milk, were added (100 µL/well) and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Following washing, species-specific IgG-HRP conjugates (rat 1:7000, dog 1:15000, rabbit 1:10000) in PBS/0.1% Tween 20/5% skim milk were applied (100 µL/well) and incubated at 37 °C for 1 h. Plates were washed, and 100 µL of TMB substrate was added, followed by a 30-minute incubation at room temperature. The reaction was stopped with 100 µL of H₂SO₄, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm using a microplate reader (BioTek, USA). Blank, negative, and positive controls were included. Positivity thresholds were established at 0.35 for rodents and 0.450 for carnivores; samples exceeding these values were classified as positive [18].

Detection of F. tularensis-specific antibodies was performed using a commercial standard tube agglutination kit (Bioveta Inc., Ivanovice, Czech Republic), incorporating pre-titrated positive and negative controls to ensure result accuracy. To mitigate potential cross-reactivity, all serum samples were also screened for brucellosis using the standard tube agglutination test (Pasteur Institute of Iran, Karaj, Iran).

sec.title: DNA preparation
sec.p: Genomic DNA was extracted from spleen and flea samples using the FavorPrep™ Tissue Genomic DNA Extraction Kit (Favorgen Biotech Corp., Taiwan) following the manufacturer’s protocol. DNA from bacterial isolates was extracted using the phenol-chloroform method [19]. DNA purity and concentration were assessed using a BioTek Epoch Microplate Spectrophotometer equipped with a Take3 Micro-Volume Plate (BioTek Instruments, Inc., USA). Absorbance was measured at 260 nm, 280 nm, and 230 nm to evaluate DNA quality. Samples with A260/A280 ratios of approximately 1.8 and A260/A230 ratios between 2.0 and 2.2 were deemed suitable for quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis. Samples outside these ranges were subjected to additional purification. All extracted DNA samples were stored at -80 °C until molecular analysis.

sec.title: Molecular assays
sec.p: Real-time PCR was performed using the TaqMan system on a Rotor-Gene™ 6600 instrument (Corbett Research Ltd., Australia) to detect specific genetic markers. Details of primers, probes, and genetic markers are provided in Table 1. Each reaction was conducted in a 20 µL volume, comprising 10 µL of 2× Real Q Plus Master Mix for Probe™ (Ampliqon Co., Denmark), 900 nM each of forward and reverse primers, 200 nM of probe, 4 µL of DNA template (1–100 ng), and double-distilled water to adjust the volume. The PCR protocol included an initial denaturation at 95 °C for 10 min, followed by 45 cycles of denaturation at 95 °C for 15 s and annealing/extension at 60 °C for 60 s for both pathogens.

Conventional PCR was employed to amplify the 16 S rRNA gene of bacterial isolates using universal primers 27 F and 1525R. PCR amplicons were purified from agarose gel using the Zymoclean™ Gel DNA Recovery Kit (Zymo Research, Irvine, CA, USA). Cycle sequencing reactions were performed using the BigDye™ Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA), and the resulting products were analyzed on an ABI 3500 Genetic Analyzer (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA, USA). Sequences were edited using CodonCode Aligner software (CodonCode Corp.) to trim low-quality bases and remove non-informative regions. Consensus sequences were generated and compared to reference sequences in the GenBank database using the BLASTn tool to identify the closest matching bacterial species.

Phylogenetic analysis was performed using jModelTest software to determine the optimal substitution model, with the HKY85 model selected based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). Phylogenetic trees were constructed using Maximum Likelihood (ML) and Neighbor Joining (NJ) methods in MEGA v7.0 software, with bootstrap analysis (1000 replicates) to evaluate tree topology reliability.

Stringent quality control measures were implemented for all molecular assays to ensure result accuracy and reliability. These included internal control templates, serial dilution controls to assess assay sensitivity, no-template controls (NTCs) to monitor contamination, and internal amplification controls to verify reaction efficiency and detect potential PCR inhibitors. Genomic DNA from Y. pestis strains and F. tularensis subsp. holarctica, sourced from the biobank, served as positive controls.

sec.title: Taxonomic overview of collected species
sec.p: A total of 65 rodents were captured, predominantly comprising black rats (Rattus rattus, n = 23, 35.38%), Indian gerbils (Tatera indica, n = 19, 29.23%), and eastern spiny mice (Acomys dimidiatus, n = 13, 20%). Seven wild carnivores were sampled, including four golden jackals (Canis aureus) and three Indian grey mongooses (Urva edwardsii). All 30 collected ectoparasites were identified as fleas of the genus Xenopsylla. Flea infestations were observed on four rodent species, with T. indica exhibiting the highest flea burden: one individual hosted 19 fleas (11 males, 8 females), another carried 8 fleas (7 males, 1 female), and a third had 2 fleas (1 male, 1 female). Additionally, a single Xenopsylla flea was collected from one Rattus norvegicus. A detailed summary of the surveyed animals and their ectoparasites is presented in Table 2.

caption.p: Wild mammals and their ectoparasites captured in Southern iran, 2018

sec.title: Bcterial isolation
sec.p: Seven bacterial isolates were obtained from the spleens of six rodents, all testing positive for a fragment of the pla gene. However, none were positive for the yihN or caf1 genes. Sequence analysis of the 16 S rRNA gene identified the bacterial species, as detailed in Table 3. All flea samples tested negative for Y. pestis. Cultures from both rodents and fleas were negative for F. tularensis.

sec.title: Microscopic analysis
sec.p: Histological sections of spleen tissues revealed no detectable Y. pestis bacilli.

sec.title: Molecular survey
sec.p: All rodent and flea samples tested negative for F. tularensis genetic markers. Nine rodents (two A. dimidiatus, two Mus musculus, two T. indica, two R. rattus, and one Meriones persicus) tested positive for a fragment of the pla gene. However, no chromosomal Y. pestis genes or the pMT1 plasmid were detected. To confirm these results, samples were re-analyzed with a new primer set, yielding consistent findings.

sec.title: Serological survey
sec.p: No rodent or wild carnivore sera exhibited detectable antibodies against Y. pestis or F. tularensis. In contrast, specific anti-Y. pestis IgG antibodies were detected in four sheepdog sera (11.42%), including one borderline result. All sheepdog sera tested negative for F. tularensis via the standard tube agglutination test.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The use of sentinel animals is a well-established strategy for the early detection of zoonotic disease outbreaks and the assessment of human exposure risk. Ideal sentinel species are susceptible to infection, survive exposure, and exhibit measurable clinical or immunological responses. Although experimental infections in dogs can induce fever and bacteremia, natural infections rarely result in clinical disease, as dogs are relatively resistant hosts. Consequently, dogs serve as effective sentinels, providing valuable insights into the plague cycle within natural ecosystems [23].

In this study, a seroprevalence of 11.42% for Y. pestis was observed in sheepdogs. Serological evidence of Y. pestis is commonly detected in dogs and cats in plague-endemic regions but is typically absent or significantly lower in plague-free areas. Due to their frequent interactions with rodents, occasional predation, and inherent resistance, dogs develop detectable IgG antibodies against the F1 capsular antigen within eight days of exposure, with antibodies persisting for up to 200 days [24, 25]. The detection of anti-Y. pestis antibodies in sheepdogs in this study indicates recent exposure to the bacterium in Hormozgan Province, highlighting a potential risk of human exposure. Given that antibody levels in dogs typically decline to undetectable levels within months, the observed seropositivity suggests ongoing circulation of Y. pestis in the region. Comparative studies in Iran, such as a 2011–2012 survey in Hamadan, western Iran, reported seropositivity in 3.4% of sheepdogs (4/117) and 1.02% of rodents (1/98) [26]. Follow-up surveillance from 2014 to 2020 in the same region found 0.32% of rodents (3/927) seropositive for Y. pestis, with no positive results in sheepdogs (n = 129), red foxes (Vulpes vulpes, n = 5), or golden jackals (Canis aureus, n = 4) [27]. Globally, seropositivity rates in dogs from plague-endemic regions vary: Ecuador 35.71% [28], China 23.5% [29], and 10% [30], Jordan 17.64% [31], Canada 9.6% [32], Tanzania 6.3% [33], 5.5% [34], 2.63% [35], and 0% [36], South Africa 5.78% [37], and 0.35% [38], Zambia 3% [39], the USA 2.09% [40], and Brazil 1.49% [41].

The plasmids pPCP1 (9.5 kb), encoding plasminogen activator protease, coagulase, and pesticin, and pMT1 (100 kb), encoding the F1 capsular antigen and murine toxin, are unique to Y. pestis and are critical for its pathogenicity [20]. These plasmids are essential for the evolutionary divergence of Y. pestis from Yersinia pseudotuberculosis. The pla (pPCP1) and caf1 (pMT1) genes are reliable molecular targets for detecting Y. pestis due to their high specificity and prevalence. However, the loss of the caf1-encoding plasmid can lead to false-negative results in diagnostic assays. Among chromosomal genes, yihN and irp2 are highly specific for Y. pestis. Most Y. pestis strains carry the pCD1, pPCP1, and pMT1 plasmids, but atypical strains lacking one or more plasmids have been identified, complicating molecular detection and increasing the risk of false negatives [42].

Recent evidence indicates that relying solely on the pla gene for Y. pestis detection may yield misleading results, as pla gene fragments have been identified in non-pathogenic bacteria such as Citrobacter koseri and Escherichia coli [43]. For example, in Algeria, an isolate positive for pla but negative for other Y. pestis-specific markers was identified as a non-pathogenic C. koseri strain [44]. Similar findings have been reported in Rattus rattus, Rattus norvegicus, Mus musculus, and Apodemus sylvaticus in regions including Canada, England, and the Netherlands [45, 46]. In this study, pla gene fragments were detected in rodent spleen isolates, but the absence of other Y. pestis-specific markers ruled out its presence, suggesting horizontal gene transfer of Y. pestis genetic elements to other gram-negative bacteria, including Citrobacter, Escherichia, Proteus, Cronobacter, Acinetobacter, and Enterobacter. These findings underscore the widespread dissemination of Y. pestis mobile genetic elements.

Antigenic similarities between Y. pestis and other gram-negative bacteria, such as Brucella spp., Y. enterocolitica, Y. pseudotuberculosis, F. tularensis, E. coli, K. pneumoniae, can lead to false-positive serological results. To mitigate cross-reactivity, highly specific diagnostic assays or confirmatory methods, such as PCR or culture-based techniques, are essential. Strategies include testing seropositive samples for cross-reactive agents, screening sera against multiple Y. pestis antigens, and employing advanced techniques like Western blot, competitive ELISA, cross-absorption tests, or blocking assays to identify cross-reactivity.

The incubation temperature for Y. pestis culturing was selected based on diagnostic objectives. Incubation at 28–30 °C optimizes bacterial growth for initial isolation [47], while 37 °C enhances expression of temperature-regulated virulence factors, such as the F1 capsular antigen encoded by caf1 [48]. A two-step incubation strategy—initial culturing at 28 °C followed by subculturing at 37 °C—was considered but not pursued, as all colonies tested negative for the yihN gene, confirming the absence of Y. pestis. Had yihN-positive colonies been detected, incubation at 37 °C would have been performed to assess F1 antigen expression.

Although no serological evidence of tularemia was detected in this study, prior studies in Iran have reported seropositivity rates of 11.11% (1/9) in southeastern Iran [49], 4.8% (8/164) [50] and 0.74% (3/407) in western Iran [51], and molecular detection rates of 1.15% (5/433) in rodents [51], 0.82% (2/244) in ticks in western Iran [4], and 2.2% (1/46) in environmental samples from northwestern Iran [52]. These findings suggest that tularemia may remain undetected in wildlife due to limited sample sizes and study durations, necessitating more comprehensive and extended investigations.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: All captured rodent species (Rattus rattus, Tatera indica, Acomys dimidiatus, and others) are potential reservoirs for Y. pestis. The detection of seropositivity in 11.42% of sheepdogs indicates recent exposure to Y. pestis and suggests a latent risk of human exposure in rural areas of Hormozgan Province. Ancient plague foci in southern Iran continue to pose a public health threat. To address this, we recommend implementing periodic surveillance for plague and other rodent-borne diseases, employing an integrated approach combining ecological, microbiological, and epidemiological strategies to ensure timely detection and effective prevention.
